name: The Pine of Viale Aldo Moro
verified_sources: MASAF/Basilicata regional register of monumental trees, sheet 03/F052/MT/17, comune di Matera, locality Viale Aldo Moro, girth 290 cm, height 22 m, flagged urban

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pino_Matera.jpg (Wiki Loves Monuments Italia 2018 entry, wiki-ID 17F05203F052MT17, camera location 40.664333,16.598019, photographed 21 September 2018, so alive and standing as of that date)
OpenStreetMap node 2505619685, tagged natural=tree, name "Il Pino", Viale Aldo Moro, Centro, Matera (40.664378, 16.598034)
access: Free. Street tree on Viale Aldo Moro, a public road; no gate or permission needed.
transport: Matera Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes on foot along Viale Aldo Moro. Piazza Vittorio Veneto and the edge of the Sassi are about 10 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: Four independent records agree on one point to within a few metres: the regional monumental-tree register (id 03/F052/MT/17, wiki-ID 17F05203F052MT17), a matching Wikidata item, a geolocated Wikimedia Commons photo from a 2018 Wiki Loves Monuments entry, and an OpenStreetMap natural=tree node that names it 'Il Pino' ('The Pine'), i.e. locals already treat it as a landmark. Species is Pinus pinea (Italian stone pine / umbrella pine), a common urban and coastal tree in Italy, distinctive umbrella-shaped crown. Girth 290 cm, height 22 m per the register. AGE: no source gives one. I looked for a growth-rate basis to derive one (published Pinus pinea DBH growth studies give roughly 1.0-1.3 cm/year in adult trees, e.g. a fertilization trial and dendrochronology papers on Italian coastal stands), but that rate is measured on already-mature trees over short (5-year) windows, not a lifetime average, and stone pines grow markedly faster as saplings; extrapolating it linearly across the tree's whole life would be exactly the kind of over-precise guess the project bans. Left age fields empty rather than force a number; the page should ask the reader if anyone knows a planting date. Wiki Loves Monuments treats the tree as a protected cultural/environmental monument, consistent with its status as a public street tree on a named avenue rather than anything private. No dead/decline signal found; the 2018 photo shows a full, healthy crown.

name: The Black Poplar of Timmari

location.address: Localita Fontana della Madonna, Colle di Timmari, Matera
location.neighbourhood: Timmari, on the Apulian-Greek archaeological park hill, about 9.5 km west of central Matera

verified_sources: MASAF/Basilicata regional register of monumental trees, sheet 07/F052/MT/17, comune di Matera, locality Colle Timmari - Fontana della Madonna, girth 420 cm, height 22 m

https://www.caimatera.it/escursione/sentiero-del-pioppo-nero-di-timmari/ (CAI Matera hiking-club excursion, run 26 January 2025, whose stated route goes to Fontana della Madonna specifically "per ammirare il pioppo nero, albero monumentale censito nel catasto regionale", i.e. an independent, non-register source confirming both the tree and this exact spot)
access: Free, on open hillside within the Timmari archaeological area. No gate, no ticket. It sits well off the beaten path: reachable on foot via forest tracks and part-paved roads through the Parco Archeologico Appulo-Greco di Timmari, and a local hiking club (CAI Matera) runs an 11 km loop trail that passes directly by it. This pass could not confirm whether a shorter direct approach by car exists; treat it as a countryside walk rather than a stroll from the Sassi.
transport: About 9.5 km / roughly a 20 minute drive west of central Matera; no public transport reaches Timmari directly. On foot from the nearest road it is a rural walk of at least an hour through the archaeological park.
verify_notes: Two independent sources: the regional monumental-tree register (girth 420 cm, height 22 m) and a Matera hiking club (CAI) excursion writeup that independently names this exact tree and place as the destination of a guided walk, describing it as census-listed in the regional cadastre. It stands at Fontana della Madonna, a spring site on the Timmari hill, beside an Apulo-Greek archaeological park (a Bronze-Age-to-classical settlement excavated by Domenico Ridola, whose finds are in Matera's archaeology museum) and near the Diga di San Giuliano reservoir. A press piece (Gazzetta del Mezzogiorno) describes Timmari as a genuinely public but poorly signposted hillside, forest trails and partly paved roads, nothing gated. SPECIES: Populus nigra, black poplar, a fast-growing native riparian species; a 420 cm girth is a substantial specimen for the species even though black poplars can put on girth quickly when young, which is exactly why I did not force an age estimate: published growth figures for the species are wildly non-linear (very fast early growth, e.g. reported ~2 m diameter in 30-50 years in temperate Europe, versus a documented maximum lifespan of up to 200 years and at least one recorded specimen dated to roughly 325 years), and this tree stands in a much drier, hotter climate than those reference figures, which would slow growth in ways I cannot quantify. Age left empty; a local with a planting record or an official dendrochronology reading is the only honest way to answer it. WORTH NOTING FOR THE STORY: the site combines a genuinely old spring-fed landscape (springs here supported settlement from the Neolithic onward) with the tree, but that is a fact about the SITE, not a bridge to the tree's own age, and should not be written as one.
